lines.s10: Cabernet Sauvignon is the firm, dark red of Bordeaux's Left Bank and of Napa: cassis, cedar and a long, drying grip.
lines.s20: Cabernet Sauvignon is the backbone of red Bordeaux and the grape Napa is known for. Expect cassis and blackberry, cedar and a firm, drying tannin that softens with age and with red meat.
lines.s45: Cabernet Sauvignon comes from the gravel of Bordeaux's Left Bank, where it leads the blend. It tastes of cassis, blackberry and black cherry, with cedar and a touch of mint. It is full bodied, with firm, drying tannin, and it keeps for decades. It is usually raised in small oak barrels, a good share of them new. Bordeaux tends to be firmer and more cedary, while Napa is typically riper, softer and fuller. It is made for red meat: a rib of beef, lamb or a dry aged steak. At a blind tasting in Paris in 1976, French judges placed a Napa Cabernet above the red Bordeaux beside it.
lines.sale: Cabernet Sauvignon has the cassis fruit and the firm grip that a fatty cut of beef calls for. Tonight I would pour it with a ribeye, and decant it while the kitchen works.

glass.lead: Cassis and blackberry over cedar and graphite, on a full body with firm, drying tannin.

ladder.where: The Médoc and Graves, Coonawarra, Margaret River
Napa Valley, Paso Robles, Maipo and the Barossa

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus, tannin high and drying, alcohol medium plus to high, body full.

old.where: Bordeaux's Left Bank, the Médoc and Graves; Bolgheri in Tuscany
old.glass: Tends to be firmer and drier in feel: cassis and redcurrant with cedar, graphite and a leafy edge of green bell pepper, moderate alcohol and tannin that needs time.
old.cellar: Nearly every wine is a blend, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and a little Petit Verdot, aged in small French oak barrels, a share of them new.

new.where: Napa Valley, Washington, Coonawarra, Margaret River, Maipo and Stellenbosch
new.glass: Typically riper and fuller: blackberry, black cherry and cassis, often with mint or eucalyptus, plusher tannin and higher alcohol. Vanilla and coffee from new oak tend to show.
new.cellar: Often bottled under the grape's own name, alone or with a little Merlot; picked riper and aged in a larger share of new oak.

contrast.why: Bordeaux's mild, damp, maritime climate ripens Cabernet only just, so it is blended and stays firm. Sunnier, drier New World sites ripen it fully. The label follows: Bordeaux names the place, the New World the grape.
contrast.blur: Coonawarra and Margaret River keep a leafy edge close to Bordeaux, while Bolgheri on the Tuscan coast and warm recent years in Bordeaux give riper, fuller wines.
contrast.call: Cedar, graphite and a dry, firm finish at moderate alcohol lean Bordeaux; ripe blackberry, mint and vanilla at higher alcohol lean New World.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius: cool room temperature, never warm.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl.
service.decant: Consider it for a young, tannic wine after tasting a sample; an old one may be decanted off its sediment.
service.age: Most open up at five to ten years; ten to thirty from a serious address.

with.dish: Ribeye or a rib of beef
with.why: fat and protein soften the tannin
the classic Médoc match, rosemary meeting the cedar
richness that needs the wine's grip and acidity
salt and fat round off the firm tannin

labels.means: Left Bank Bordeaux place names: the label names the village, and Cabernet Sauvignon leads the blend.
Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and sometimes Petit Verdot or Malbec, wherever it is made.
A classed growth: an estate ranked in the Médoc classification of 1855.
An American name for blends of the Bordeaux grapes, not a legal category; it rhymes with heritage.

guest.q: Why does this Cabernet dry my mouth out?
guest.a: That is tannin, from the grape's thick skins and from oak. It grips most when the wine is young, and it softens with air, with age and with a fatty cut of meat.
Red Bordeaux is a blend. On the Left Bank, in the Médoc and Graves, Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads; on the Right Bank, Merlot does.
For a young, firm bottle it often helps, and I can pour you a taste first. For an old one I would decant gently to leave the sediment behind.

compare.tell: Merlot is softer and rounder, with plum where Cabernet has cassis, and less of the drying grip and cedar.
Cabernet Franc, its parent, is lighter and more fragrant: raspberry, violet and pencil shavings, with a leafier edge and gentler tannin.
Syrah brings cracked black pepper, smoked meat and black olive; Cabernet has cassis and cedar and a firmer, more drying tannin.

cards.front: Cabernet Sauvignon: its two parents, and where it is at home?
cards.back: Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, shown by DNA work published in 1997. Home is the gravel of Bordeaux's Left Bank: the Médoc and Graves.

cards.front: Cabernet Sauvignon blind: Bordeaux or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Cedar, graphite and a dry, firm finish at moderate alcohol lean Bordeaux. Riper blackberry, mint, vanilla and higher alcohol lean Napa, Coonawarra or Maipo.

cards.front: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon age, and what does age bring?
cards.back: Small berries with thick skins give high tannin and deep colour. With years the tannin softens and tobacco leaf, cigar box and leather appear.

questions.q: Two glasses of Cabernet Sauvignon are poured blind. One is cedary and firm at moderate alcohol, the other riper, with mint, vanilla and higher alcohol. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Cedar, graphite and firm tannin at moderate alcohol tend to mark Left Bank Bordeaux. Riper fruit, mint, vanilla from new oak and higher alcohol tend to mark a warm New World site such as Napa.

questions.q: A guest orders a young Pauillac with a rib of beef and asks why you suggest decanting it. What is the reason?
opts: Air can open the aroma of a young, firm wine
It takes the tannin out of the wine
It warms the wine to room temperature
questions.exp: Decanting a young, tannic red gives it air, which can open the aroma and ease the first impression of tannin. It does not remove tannin, and a sample tells you whether it helps.

questions.q: A guest asks where Cabernet Sauvignon came from. Which two grapes are its parents?
questions.exp: DNA work at the University of California, Davis, published in 1997, showed a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, a surprise because one parent is white.
